statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: No. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires suspicious activity reporting by financial institutions, and the facts do not establish that any covered financial institution had a SAR-filing obligation triggered by these transactions.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates that a covered financial institution report suspicious transactions (i.e., file a SAR) under Treasury regulations when the institution detects facts that may involve illegal activity, BSA evasion, or lack an apparent lawful purpose. Element-by-element: (1) Covered actor: § 5318(g) applies to a “financial institution” (as defined/implemented by BSA regulations). The fact pattern describes Entity SYN_33b1fb8b as an import-export trading business, not a bank/MSB/broker-dealer or other covered financial institution, and it does not identify any specific financial institution involved. (2) Reporting trigger: while the listed wires/ACHs are large and frequent, the facts provide no indication of suspected illegality, structuring/BSA evasion, or other suspicious indicators beyond volume, and do not state that any institution formed the requisite suspicion. (3) Duty to report: because the record does not show a covered financial institution or a regulatory SAR trigger determination, it is not possible to conclude the statute applies on these facts. Contiguous phrase in answer: “§ 5318(g) requires suspicious”.
